unit.unitOverview: Communication means presenting information clearly, by speaking or writing, and also listening carefully to others and asking good questions about what they say. It has two halves that always work together: presenting your ideas so that someone else can follow them, and listening so that you really understand what others tell you back.

explainers.title: Hello, and welcome to your final unit
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to the last unit of your Global Perspectives year at Ehel Academy. You have grown five thinking skills already, one at a time, and here they all are together:

This unit is about the sixth and final skill: Communication. It is a wonderful skill to finish on, because it is where all your other work finally goes out into the world. You can research a topic carefully, analyse it, and judge it well, but none of that helps anyone else until you can share it clearly.

Why does this matter beyond school? Think about the grown-ups around you. A shopkeeper explaining a new price to a customer. A health worker telling a family how to keep a wound clean. All of them are communicating: presenting information clearly, and listening to the people who answer back. A learner who practises this now will be heard, and able to help others, for the whole of their life.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, tidy way.
Analysis — looking closely at a topic and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an idea or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you change your mind.
Collaboration — working well together with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so that others understand you.

explainers.title: So what is communication?
explainers.body:
Many people think communication just means talking. It is more than that. Communication means presenting information so that others can understand it, whether you speak it or write it. It also means listening to others when they present, and asking a good question when something is not clear. So communication always has two halves that work together.

A good communicator is strong at both halves. If you only present, you miss what others know, and you cannot answer the questions they ask. If you only listen, your own good ideas stay locked inside your head. This unit grows both halves, so that you can share an issue and truly talk it over with other people.
bullets: Presenting — sending your ideas out clearly, by speaking or writing, so that a listener or reader can follow them.
Listening — taking in what others send you, and asking a question when something is not clear.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in the Ehel Academy way, which means three kinds of support work together.

In the old style of this subject, learners were simply told to 'present to the class' or 'talk to a partner'. In our way, you do something better first. You rehearse with your AI tutor, as many times as you like. The tutor listens to your presentation, plays the part of your audience, asks you the questions a real listener might ask, and gives you kind, honest feedback. Then, when you are ready, you deliver it for real: to your teacher in your live session, and to your family at home.

Every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box in this unit, treat it as a real rehearsal. Do not worry if presenting feels a little scary at first. Almost everyone feels that way, and rehearsing with your tutor is exactly how that feeling shrinks.
bullets: You, at your own pace. You read, think and complete the activities in your own time.
Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. In this unit your AI tutor has a special job: it is your audience and your rehearsal partner.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you deliver your best work for real, to a real audience.

explainers.title: Meet Samatar, who wants to be heard
explainers.body:
All year we have followed learners at Ehel Academy across the Horn of Africa. For this final unit, meet Samatar, a Grade 5 learner at Ehel Academy in Burao.

Samatar likes to think a problem through fully before he opens his mouth, so when his class votes on an idea quickly, his hand often goes up last. But he has an idea he cares about, and this time he is determined to be heard.

Every evening, once his little brother falls asleep, Samatar tries to finish his reading in the last hour of daylight. On some evenings the family has no oil left for the lamp, and the words go blurry as the light fades. Samatar has noticed the same thing happening to friends across his neighbourhood: homework left half-finished, and books he loves left unread, simply because the sun went down first.

Samatar's idea is that Ehel Academy could lend out a small number of solar lamps: each one charges in the sun during the school day, a child carries it home overnight to study, and it is returned each morning to charge again. He wants the school's leaders to agree to try it, the younger children to understand how borrowing works and why the rules matter, and his own family to see why he is proud of the idea. Presenting to three different audiences, and listening carefully to each one, is exactly what this final skill is for. As you meet each new communication skill, you will watch exactly how Samatar builds and delivers his case. By the end, he will stand up in front of real people and be heard, and you will be doing the very same thing.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: communicating what matters
explainers.body:
Your Challenge for this unit is to communicate an issue you care about so clearly, and so fairly, that others understand it and want to help. You will build a short presentation, rehearse it with your AI tutor, and deliver it for real. Here are three good issues to communicate about. Any of them could be your Challenge:

Your classmates will care about different things. Amina wants the tuck shop to sell more fruit and fewer sweets. Yusuf thinks the acacia trees that shade the football pitch should be protected from being cut for firewood. Any of these could grow into a strong Challenge.

You do not have to choose this very moment. As you meet each skill, keep a note of any issue you would love other people to understand and act on. That feeling, wanting to be heard about something that matters, is the heart of communication.
bullets: Lending solar lamps for evening study. Should Ehel Academy lend out a small number of solar lamps, so that children without light at home can study after dark? This is Samatar's Challenge, and a good one for a clear, fair case.
A fairer tuck shop. Should the school tuck shop sell more fruit and fewer sweets, for the health of every learner? This has clear reasons on more than one side.

Protecting the shade trees. Is there a rule that would protect the acacia trees around the football pitch, so there is still shade for children in ten years' time? Presenting a case about a rule is exactly what communication is for.

explainers.title: Starting: presenting clearly and listening well
explainers.body: The first two skills are the foundation of everything else. They are the two halves of communication in their simplest form: telling others about an issue clearly, and listening to what they tell you back.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Presenting information clearly
explainers.body:
To present means to share information with other people so that they understand it. You can present by speaking, such as giving a short talk, or by writing, such as writing a clear notice. The goal is always the same: the person on the other side should end up understanding your idea just as you do.

Three simple habits make any presentation clearer:
bullets: Start by saying what your issue is, so your audience knows what you are talking about before you dive in.
Take one idea at a time, in a sensible order, instead of jumping about.
Use a real example, because an example makes an idea easy to picture and remember.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Telling others about an issue, and listening so you understand
explainers.body:
Real communication is a two-way street. You tell others about your issue, and you listen to what they tell you, and when something is unclear you ask a question. Listening well is a skill in itself: it means paying full attention, noticing the important parts, and asking about anything you did not quite catch.

Many issues have more than one side, with reasons for and reasons that worry people. A reason someone gives to support their view is called an argument. When people share their reasons and listen to each other's, everyone understands the issue far better than they did alone.

explainers.title: Developing: building a clear case
explainers.body: Now you move from simply telling and listening to building a case: finding your strongest reasons, planning a clear structure, referring to your sources, and thinking about the people you want to reach.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Finding the arguments and evidence in a source
explainers.body:
Before you can present a good case, you need good material. A useful skill is to read a source, such as a short article or a notice, and pull out its arguments and the evidence that supports each one. An argument is the reason; the supporting evidence is the fact, detail or example that backs it up. A strong argument always has support behind it; a weak one is just a claim with nothing behind it.

A neat way to do this is to make two columns: one for each argument you find, and one for the supporting idea or example beside it.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Making a skeleton plan
explainers.body:
A presentation without a plan wanders, and a wandering talk loses its audience. So before you write or speak, you make a skeleton plan: a simple frame that shows the order of your ideas, like the bones that hold a body upright. A good skeleton for a clear, fair presentation has four parts, in this order:

Notice the third part. You do not hide a worry people might have; you name it fairly, and then answer it. This makes your case feel fairer, and, oddly, more convincing, because your audience can see you have thought about more than just your own side.
bullets: Introduction — say what the issue is, and what you think.
Reasons — your strongest reasons, with where each idea came from.
A concern, answered fairly — one worry people might have, stated fairly, and your answer to it.
Conclusion — sum up, and say clearly what you want to happen.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Referring to your sources
explainers.body:
A strong presenter refers to their sources. When you use a fact, you say where it came from. This does two things: it shows you are not just making things up, and it lets your audience trust and check your work.

You can refer to a source in a simple, spoken way, without it sounding stiff or difficult.
bullets: According to a health notice at the clinic, reading in poor light can tire your eyes.
In my own survey of fifteen classmates, nine of them had no light to read by after dark.
A teacher told me that a solar lamp fully charges in one sunny school day.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Thinking about your audience
explainers.body:
Your audience is the people you are presenting to, and a clever communicator always asks: who am I trying to reach, and what do they already care about? Different audiences care about different things, so the same case can be shared in different ways.

You do not change your facts for different audiences. You change which reasons you lead with, and which examples you choose, so that your case connects with what that audience cares about most.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Using facts and opinions, and hearing the other side
explainers.body:
A believable case is built from both facts and opinions, and a good communicator knows the difference. A fact is something that can be checked and shown to be true. An opinion is what someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with. You need both: facts make your case solid, and opinions show what you believe and why it matters.

The most convincing communicators do one more brave thing: they hear the other side. They say, honestly, what a worried person might think, and then they answer it. Far from weakening your case, this makes your audience trust you more, because you are clearly being fair.
bullets: Fact: Solar lamps charge in sunlight during the school day. This can be checked, so it is a fact.
Opinion: Solar lamps are the best invention for a school like ours. This is a belief, so it is an opinion.

explainers.title: Getting better: listening and asking relevant questions
explainers.body: The final skill returns to the second half of communication: listening. A skilled communicator is not only a clear speaker but a sharp, kind listener who asks relevant questions, the kind that help everyone understand an issue more deeply.

explainers.title: Skill 8: Active listening and asking relevant questions
explainers.body:
Active listening means listening with full attention, on purpose. You watch the speaker, you follow their idea, and you note the parts you want to ask about. Then, when they finish, you respond with a relevant question: one that is truly about what they said, and that helps you understand or gently test their idea. Three kinds of question are especially useful:

Good questions are a gift to a speaker, not an attack. Asking 'How do you know that?' in a kind voice helps the speaker show their evidence, and helps everyone listening decide how much to trust the idea.
bullets: To understand: Could you explain what you mean by that?
To go deeper: What do you mean by 'not enough' light, exactly?
To test the idea: How do you know that? Where did that fact come from?

explainers.title: How communication draws on your other skills
explainers.body:
Communication is the last skill for a reason: it gathers up every skill you have grown this year and sends it out into the world. Look how each earlier skill lives inside a good presentation:

So communication is not a brand-new skill sitting on its own. It is the moment all six skills work together. Every hour you spent researching, analysing, evaluating, reflecting and collaborating this year now pays off, because it is the strong thinking behind a message worth hearing.
bullets: Research gives you the facts and sources you refer to, so your case is believable and not just a feeling.
Analysis gives you the reasons, causes and consequences that make up the body of your case.
Evaluation helps you judge which reasons and sources are strong enough to use, and which to drop.
Reflection helps you notice how your own view has changed, and answer the question 'why do you think that?' honestly.
Collaboration taught you to listen to others and value their perspectives, which is the whole second half of communicating.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: communicating your whole Challenge
explainers.body: You have now met every communication skill in this unit. Here is how they fit together into one smooth path you can follow to communicate any Challenge:
bullets: Choose your issue and decide what you think about it.
Read your sources and pull out the arguments and their supporting evidence.
Choose your strongest reasons.
Build a skeleton plan: introduction, reasons, a concern answered fairly, conclusion.
Think about your audience and who you want to reach.
Refer to your sources, and use facts and opinions honestly.
Hear the other side fairly, and answer it.
Rehearse with your AI tutor, then deliver it for real to your teacher and your family.
Listen to the questions people ask, and answer them, asking your own relevant questions in return.

explainers.title: You have completed your Stage 5 skills journey
explainers.body:
Look back at how far you have come this year. You began by learning to research the world carefully. You learned to analyse an issue into its causes and effects, to evaluate how strong different ideas and sources really are, to reflect honestly on your own learning, and to collaborate kindly with a team. And now, with communication, you have learned to share all of that clearly and fairly, and to be heard.

These six skills are yours to keep. They are not just for Global Perspectives, or even for school. They are the skills of a thoughtful, fair and useful person: someone who finds things out, thinks them through, works well with others, and speaks up for what matters. You will use them for the rest of your life.

Well done for finishing your Stage 5 journey. Be proud of the thinker you have become, and get ready to grow these six skills even further in the years ahead.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a bus, and the skill is where the bus takes you.
We will use real topics such as solar lamps, the tuck shop and the shade trees.
But the real prize is not the topic. It is to become a clear, fair communicator who could present almost any idea, and listen well to almost anyone.

bigIdeas.title: The two halves of communication
lines: Presenting: How can I share my ideas so that others understand them clearly?
Listening: When others present, what question can I ask to understand them better?
Every strong communicator keeps swapping between these two halves, like a good game of catch.

bigIdeas.title: Being fair to every perspective
lines: In any community, people hold different views, shaped by their family and their circumstances.
One family has a solar panel at home already; another has never had electric light at all; a shopkeeper worries about the cost of the lamps.
A fair communicator represents these perspectives honestly, even the ones they disagree with, and never pretends a whole community thinks one way.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Choose one issue you would love other people to understand and act on. This is your Challenge.
You will build a presentation about it, step by step, and deliver it at the end.
Pick something you truly care about, because it is much easier to speak well about what matters to you.

In the old style of Global Perspectives you would 'present to the class' once and hope it went well. In the Ehel Academy model you rehearse as many times as you like with your AI tutor, which plays your audience and asks the questions a real listener might, until your case is clear and you feel ready. Only then do you deliver it for real, to your teacher and to people at home.

bigIdeas.title: Source: Should Ehel Academy start a lamp-lending scheme?
lines: In Burao, and in many towns across the Horn of Africa, some homes have electric light in the evening and some do not. Children who have no light at home find it hard to read or finish their homework once the sun goes down.

Some people think the school should lend out small solar lamps. Each lamp charges in the sun during the school day, then a child can take it home overnight to study, and bring it back in the morning to charge again. They say this would help many more children finish their homework, and enjoy reading for pleasure too.

Other people are not sure. A solar lamp costs money, and the school does not have very many. Some worry that a lamp could be lost, dropped or not returned, and then fewer children could use it. Someone would need to keep a fair list of whose turn it is.

bigIdeas.title: Persuasive openers you can borrow
lines: Imagine a ... where ...
Every evening, ...
Surely we all want ...
It is time to ...

Read your opening aloud to yourself, because a presentation is meant to be heard, not just seen on the page. If it sounds clear and lively when you say it, it will work well in front of a real audience.

bigIdeas.title: Good questions to ask a speaker
lines: Could you explain what you mean by ...?
What do you mean by ...?
How do you know that? Where did that come from?
Can you tell me a little more about that?

bigIdeas.title: What good listeners do
lines: Make eye contact with the speaker, and keep still and quiet while they talk.
Let the speaker finish before you speak.
Notice the parts you want to ask about, so your question is ready.
When they finish, ask a relevant question or add an idea of your own.

models.title: A model skeleton plan you can copy the shape of
lines: Introduction: not every family at Ehel Academy has light to read by after dark, and I think the school should lend out solar lamps.
Reasons: a lamp charges for free in the sun, and my own survey of fifteen classmates found that nine of them had no light to read by in the evening.
A concern, answered fairly: it is true that a lamp could be lost or not returned. However, a simple sign-out list, one lamp per family per week, would make it fair and easy to track.
Conclusion: let us trial five lamps for one term, so every child gets a fair turn to study after dark.

models.title: A model: answering a concern fairly
lines: The concern, stated fairly: it is true that the school only has a little money to spend, and lamps are not free.
The answer: however, five lamps would cost less than the school already spends on paper in a month, and every child would get a fair turn through a sign-out list.
Notice how answering the worry, instead of ignoring it, makes the case stronger and fairer.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 6 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Communication. This is my last unit of the year.
Ask it: In one or two simple sentences, why is it not enough to find out about an issue, if I cannot share it with others?
Then tell your tutor whether you find presenting or listening harder, and why. Ask it to be your rehearsal partner for this whole unit.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one issue you care about, then present it in three sentences: what the issue is, what you think, and one reason.
Ask the tutor to be your listener and tell you, honestly, whether it understood your issue from your three sentences.
Ask: which sentence was the clearest, and which one should I make simpler?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Pick an issue with more than one side. Tell your AI tutor one reason for it, and one worry someone might have.
Ask the tutor to play someone who holds the opposite view to yours, and share their reason out loud.
Listen carefully, then tell the tutor its reason back in your own words, and ask: did I understand you correctly?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Find or recall a short source about your issue. Tell your AI tutor two arguments it makes.
For each argument, tell the tutor the supporting evidence, the fact or example that backs it up.
Ask: which of my arguments has the strongest support, and which one is a bit empty?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your issue and what you think about it.
Ask it to help you fill a skeleton plan: introduction, reasons, a concern answered fairly, conclusion.
Then ask: does my order flow well, and is my concern stated fairly?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present one fact about your issue to your AI tutor, and say where it came from.
Ask the tutor whether it was easy to trust your fact, and why.
Ask it to suggest one more source you could refer to, to make your case stronger.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the different audiences you want to reach with your case.
Ask it to help you decide which of your reasons would matter most to each audience, and why.
Then ask the tutor to play one of those audiences, so you can practise leading with a different reason.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one fact and one opinion from your case, and check you have labelled each correctly.
Ask the tutor to raise a worry about your idea, as strongly as it can.
Practise acknowledging its point fairly, then answering it, and ask the tutor whether your answer was convincing.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to present a short case for a solution to a local issue, as if it were a classmate.
Listen actively and jot notes, then ask it two relevant questions: one to understand, and one to test the idea.
Ask the tutor to rate your questions and suggest one even sharper question you could have asked.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your issue, and who you most want to influence.
Ask it: is my issue a good size to present in a few minutes, or is it too big?
Ask the tutor to help you say what you think in one clear, confident sentence.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your arguments and supporting evidence to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you matched the right evidence to each argument.
Then tell it the arguments for your OWN issue, and ask which ones have the strongest support.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your full list of reasons to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you pick your two or three strongest, and to explain any it would choose differently.
Ask: which of my reasons would matter most to the audience I want to reach?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four-part skeleton plan to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your order flows well and your concern is stated fairly.
Ask the tutor to check that your conclusion ends with a clear, doable action.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two facts and their sources to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your structure was easy to follow, and where you referred to a source well.
Ask it to suggest one more way to refer to a source out loud.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which reason you would lead with for each of your three audiences.
Ask it whether your choices make sense, and why.
Then ask the tutor to play one audience, so you can practise presenting to them.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your facts, your opinion, and your answer to the concern to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check that your facts really are facts and your opinion really is an opinion.
Ask the tutor to raise the concern back at you, so you can practise answering it out loud.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your whole case to your AI tutor from start to finish.
Ask it to be your audience and give you two stars and one wish: two things that worked and one thing to improve.
Then ask the tutor to tell your talk back to you, so you can check your key message came through clearly.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: After your listening practice, ask your AI tutor to rate your questions: were they relevant and clear?
Ask it to suggest one sharper question you could have asked.
Ask the tutor why asking 'How do you know that?' kindly can help a whole group, not just you.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your fact-or-opinion answers and your fixed sentence to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your rewrite stayed honest, keeping the same facts.
Ask the tutor to show you one more way to make a flat sentence clearer.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your quiz answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to tell you which answer was the strongest, and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more scenario like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your whole-year reflection to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how much you have grown across all six skills since the start of the year.
Ask the tutor to suggest one skill to carry forward and keep sharpening, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: A human touch
lines: Ask someone at home which local issue they most wish more people understood.
Listen carefully to their answer, then tell them one issue you might present about this unit.
Bring both ideas to your next teacher session. The issues the adults around you care about often make the strongest Challenges.

speakingPrompts.title: Samatar introduces his idea clearly
lines: Samatar begins his talk with one clear sentence: Not every family at our school has light to read by after dark, and I think we should try lending out solar lamps.
In one breath, his audience knows exactly what the issue is.
He then gives one idea at a time: first the problem, then his idea, then why it would help. Nobody gets lost.
Notice that clear presenting is not about big words or a loud voice. It is about order and care: knowing what you want to say, and helping the other person follow it step by step.

speakingPrompts.title: Samatar listens to a worry, and asks a good question back
lines: When Samatar first shares his idea with his teacher, she says: I worry a lamp might get lost.
Samatar does not argue straight away. He listens fully, then asks: What would make you feel it was safe to try?
His teacher explains that a simple sign-out list would help. Samatar writes this down, because it will make his plan fairer and stronger.

When you listen, you do not have to agree straight away. You are simply trying to understand, so that later you can answer fairly. A good listener can often explain the other person's worry back to them, which is one of the surest signs that real communication has happened.

speakingPrompts.title: Samatar pulls the arguments out of a source about lamps
lines: Samatar reads a short notice about solar lamp schemes at other schools.
Argument: lamps help children finish homework. Supporting evidence: at one school, more children handed in finished homework after lamps were introduced.
Argument: lamps cost little to run. Supporting evidence: they charge for free in sunlight, with no oil or batteries needed.
Samatar also notes a worry on the other side: some schools found lamps went missing until they kept a proper list.
Reading a source this way makes you a sharper communicator, because you learn to separate a solid, supported argument from a weak, empty one.

speakingPrompts.title: Samatar refers to his sources as he presents
lines: When Samatar says many children have no light at home, he adds: in my own survey of fifteen classmates, nine of them told me the same thing.
When he says a lamp costs little, he adds: a teacher told me it charges fully in one sunny school day.
By naming where each fact came from, Samatar turns his opinion into a case his audience can believe.

speakingPrompts.title: Samatar adapts his case for three audiences
lines: For the school leaders, Samatar leads with the cost being small and the plan being fair and easy to manage.
For the younger children, he leads with how the lamp works and the simple rule: borrow it, use it carefully, bring it back in the morning.
For his family, he leads with how proud he is that his own idea could help other families like his.
The facts stay the same. Only the order and the examples change, so each audience feels the case is about them.

speakingPrompts.title: Samatar answers a concern fairly
lines: Fact, with a source: my survey found that nine of fifteen classmates had no light to read by after dark.
Opinion: I think a fair sign-out list would make this plan work well for our school.
The concern, acknowledged: it is true that lamps could get lost or broken.
His answer: however, a simple list, with one lamp per family per week, would make it fair and easy to track.
When you acknowledge a concern, use fair, respectful words: 'It is true that ...', 'Some people worry that ...'. Then answer with 'However,' or 'Even so,'.

speakingPrompts.title: Samatar listens to a younger child's question
lines: A Grade 1 child asks Samatar: how does the lamp get its light if there is no plug?
Samatar listens fully to the question, then explains simply: the lamp has a small panel that catches sunlight all day, and stores it inside, like filling a cup with water.
The child nods, then asks a follow-up: can I keep it forever? Samatar answers kindly, and explains the sign-out rule, so the lamp gets shared fairly.
Listening carefully to a question, even a simple one, and answering it honestly, is exactly what good communication looks like.

speakingPrompts.title: Deliver it for real
lines: Bring your presentation to your next teacher session and deliver it to a real audience.
Afterwards, present it to your family or a neighbour, and ask them what they understood and what they would ask.
Write down one thing that went well, and one thing you will do even better next time.

speakingPrompts.title: Samatar's whole journey, from a dark room to being heard
lines: Skills 1 and 2: He learned to present his issue clearly, and to listen to a worry and ask a question about it.
Skills 3 and 4: He pulled arguments and evidence from a source, and built a skeleton plan with his strongest reasons.
Skills 5 and 6: He referred to his own survey and a teacher's fact, and adapted his case for school leaders, younger children and his family.
Skills 7 and 8: He used facts and opinions honestly, answered a concern fairly, and listened actively to questions, including a younger child's.

By following this path, Samatar turned a quiet evening worry into a clear, fair case, and he delivered it to real people who could help. That is communication doing its true job: not just knowing something, but helping others understand it and act.

starting: tell someone about an issue that matters to me, in a clear order
listen to what someone tells me about an issue, and ask them a question about it
developing: present information about my issue with a clear structure, and say where my ideas came from
listen to ideas and information about an issue, and ask a question that is relevant to it
gettingBetter: present my information clearly, in a sensible order, referring to my sources where that helps
listen carefully to ideas and information about an issue, then ask the questions that matter to it

toolkit.title: The Communication skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Communication means presenting information so that others can understand it, by speaking or writing, and also listening carefully to others and asking good questions. It has two halves that always work together: presenting your ideas clearly, and listening so you truly understand what others say back.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, be clear: know what you want to say, put it in a sensible order, and support it with facts and sources. Second, be fair: listen to other people, answer their concerns, and never pretend a whole community thinks one way. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: The two halves of communication
toolkit.intro: Communication is always two things at once. A strong communicator keeps swapping between them, like a good game of catch. Keep both in mind whenever you plan a presentation or take part in a discussion.

rows: Presenting
Sending your ideas out clearly, by speaking or writing.
Say what your issue is, then give one idea at a time, with an example.
Listening
Taking in what others send you, and asking about anything unclear.
Pay full attention, note the key points, then ask a relevant question.

toolkit.title: Your Stage 5 Communication learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your communication skills grow in three stages this year: starting, developing, and getting better. Here are the real Cambridge learning goals for this stage, in simple words. Your teacher may talk about these.

rows: Communicating information
Present your information clearly, in a sensible order, mentioning where your facts came from.
Listening and responding
Listen carefully to ideas and information about an issue, and ask the questions that matter to it.

toolkit.title: Template: the skeleton plan
toolkit.intro: Copy this template to plan any clear, fair presentation. Fill each row with your own idea, and note beside it where the idea came from, so you can refer to your sources.

rows: Introduction
Name the issue and say what you think.
Reasons
Your strongest reasons, with where each idea came from.
A concern, answered fairly
One worry people might have, stated fairly, and your answer to it.
Conclusion
Sum up, and say the one thing you want to happen.

toolkit.title: Referring to your sources
toolkit.intro: Use these to show where your facts came from, so your audience can trust and check your work.
items: According to ... (a notice, a website, a person who knows the topic)
In my own survey of ... classmates, I found that ...
A teacher, a parent or an expert told me that ...
I read that ..., and I checked it against ...

toolkit.title: Persuasive language and sentence starters
toolkit.intro:
Use these to make a true idea clear and vivid. Persuasive language should make honest ideas shine, never make a false idea seem true.

To acknowledge a concern fairly, use: It is true that ... , Some people worry that ... , and then answer with However, ... or Even so, ...
items: Paint a picture: Imagine a ... where ...
Speak to the audience: Surely we all want ...
Ask a question: Is this really how we want to ...?
Call for action: It is time to ... The first step is simple.
Add weight: Not only ... but also ...

toolkit.title: Facts and opinions
toolkit.intro: A strong case uses both: facts make it solid, and opinions show what you believe and why it matters. Always say where a fact came from.

rows: Fact
Something that can be checked and shown to be true.
Solar lamps charge in sunlight.
Opinion
What someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.
Solar lamps are the best invention for our school.

toolkit.title: Good questions to ask a speaker
toolkit.intro:
When you listen to a presentation, respond with relevant questions. These help you understand the idea and gently test how strong it is.

Ask kindly. A good question is a gift that helps the speaker show their evidence and helps the whole group understand.
items: To understand: Could you explain what you mean by ...?
To go deeper: What do you mean by ...?
To test the idea: How do you know that? Where did that come from?
To hear more: Can you tell me a little more about that?

toolkit.title: How to rehearse with your AI tutor
toolkit.intro:
Your AI tutor is your audience and your rehearsal partner. Use it like this, as often as you need, until your case feels clear and you feel calm.

Rehearsing in private is how nervous speakers become confident ones. Nobody sees your early, wobbly attempts except a patient tutor, so you can make all your mistakes safely, long before you stand up in front of real people.
items: Present your whole case to the tutor from start to finish, out loud if you can.
Ask it to be your audience and give you two stars and a wish: two things that worked, and one to improve.
Ask it to tell your talk back to you, so you can check that your key message came through.
Ask it to raise a concern, so you can practise answering it calmly.
Improve one thing, then present again. Repeat until you feel ready to deliver it for real.

toolkit.title: Delivering with confidence
toolkit.intro:
When you deliver for real, in your teacher session or at home, how you speak matters as much as what you say. These simple habits help your audience listen.

You will not get all of these right at once, and that is fine. Pick just one to focus on each time you rehearse, and it will slowly become a habit you no longer have to think about.
items: Slow down. Speak a little more slowly than feels natural, so every word is clear.
Pause. Stop for a moment after your key message, to let it land.
Look up. Glance at your audience, not only at your page.
Breathe. A slow breath before you start steadies a nervous voice.

toolkit.title: Signpost words for a clear structure
toolkit.intro: Signpost words tell your audience where they are in your talk, so nobody gets lost. Sprinkle a few of these through your presentation.
items: To begin: Today I want to talk about ... , First ...
To add a reason: In addition ... , Another reason is ...
To turn to a concern: Some people worry that ... , However ...
To conclude: So, to sum up ... , This is why ... , The one thing I am asking for is ...

toolkit.title: Two stars and a wish
toolkit.intro: When your AI tutor, your teacher or a family member gives you feedback, ask for it in a kind, useful shape: two stars and a wish. The two stars are two things that worked well. The wish is the one thing that would make it even better. Give feedback to others the same way. It keeps everyone brave enough to keep trying, and it always leaves the speaker with one clear thing to improve next time.

checklists.title: Checklist: Is my presentation clear and strong?
checklists.intro: Tick each one before you deliver. If you cannot tick them all, go back and improve that part.
items: Structure — it has a clear introduction, reasons and conclusion, in a sensible order.
Facts and opinions — I use facts I can check, and I make my own opinions clear.
Sources — I say where my facts came from.
A concern — I fairly state one worry people might have, and I answer it.
Audience — I lead with the reasons that matter most to the people I want to reach.

challenge.intro:
You have now built and delivered a real piece of communication. Pull it together by completing these three sentences about your Challenge, in your own words:

Keep this checkpoint safe. You will look back at it during Reflection, where you will think not just about this unit, but about your whole year of six skills.
checkpoints: The message I most wanted people to understand was ...
When I delivered it, I was proud that ...
One thing I would do differently next time is ...

activities.title: Choose your issue and your audience
activities.label: Activity 1: Choose your issue and your audience
activities.intro:
Every presentation starts with a clear issue and a clear audience. Look back at the three ideas in the Lesson file (lending solar lamps, a fairer tuck shop, or protecting the shade trees), or choose your own.

Knowing who you most want to reach makes everything easier. It does not have to be one single person; it can be a group, such as the school's leaders or the younger children.
steps: Write your issue in one sentence: 'The issue I want to communicate is ...'.
Write one sentence saying who you most want to influence, and why they should care.
Write one sentence saying what you think about it.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your issue, and who you most want to influence.
Ask it: is my issue a good size to present in a few minutes, or is it too big?
Ask the tutor to help you say what you think in one clear, confident sentence.

activities.title: Analyse a source for arguments and evidence
activities.label: Activity 2: Analyse a source for arguments and evidence
activities.intro:
A strong case is built from strong arguments. Read the short source below about a lamp-lending scheme at Ehel Academy. Your job is to pull out its arguments and the supporting evidence for each one.

Making two columns can help: one for each argument, and one for the supporting ideas or examples beside it. A supported argument is far stronger than a bare claim.
steps: Write down two arguments FOR the lamp-lending scheme, and the supporting evidence for each.
Write down one argument AGAINST, or one worry, and the evidence or reason behind it.
Which single argument do you find the most persuasive, and why?

boxes.title: Source: Should Ehel Academy start a lamp-lending scheme?
lines: In Burao, and in many towns across the Horn of Africa, some homes have electric light in the evening and some do not. Children who have no light at home find it hard to read or finish their homework once the sun goes down.

Some people think the school should lend out small solar lamps. Each lamp charges in the sun during the school day, then a child can take it home overnight to study, and bring it back in the morning to charge again. They say this would help many more children finish their homework, and enjoy reading for pleasure too.

Other people are not sure. A solar lamp costs money, and the school does not have very many. Some worry that a lamp could be lost, dropped or not returned, and then fewer children could use it. Someone would need to keep a fair list of whose turn it is.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your arguments and supporting evidence to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you matched the right evidence to each argument.
Then tell it the arguments for your OWN issue, and ask which ones have the strongest support.

activities.title: Choose your strongest reasons
activities.label: Activity 3: Choose your strongest reasons
activities.intro:
Now gather the reasons for your own issue and choose only the strongest. A few powerful reasons persuade far better than a long list of weak ones.

It can feel strange to leave out reasons you worked hard to find. Do it anyway. An audience remembers two or three strong reasons far better than eight weak ones.
steps: List every reason you can think of that supports your idea.
Choose the two or three most persuasive. For each, write why it is strong.
Cross out any weak reason, and write one sentence saying why you dropped it.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your full list of reasons to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you pick your two or three strongest, and to explain any it would choose differently.
Ask: which of my reasons would matter most to the audience I want to reach?

activities.title: Build your skeleton plan
activities.label: Activity 4: Build your skeleton plan
activities.intro:
Time to give your case its bones. A skeleton plan sets the order of your ideas, so your audience can follow you. Use the four-part shape you met in the Lesson file.

Beside each point, jot where the idea came from, so you can refer to your sources when you present. Keep this skeleton plan safe: it is the frame for everything you write and say next.
steps: Introduction: write one line naming your issue and what you think.
Reasons: your strongest reasons, with where each idea came from.
A concern, answered fairly: one worry people might have, stated fairly, and your answer.
Conclusion: sum up, and write the one thing you want to happen.

boxes.title: A model skeleton plan you can copy the shape of
lines: Introduction: not every family at our school has light to read by after dark, and I think the school should lend out solar lamps.
Reasons: a lamp charges for free in the sun, and my own survey of fifteen classmates found that nine of them had no light to read by in the evening.
A concern, answered fairly: it is true that a lamp could be lost or not returned. However, a simple sign-out list, one lamp per family per week, would make it fair and easy to track.
Conclusion: let us trial five lamps for one term, so every child gets a fair turn to study after dark.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four-part skeleton plan to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your order flows well and your concern is stated fairly.
Ask the tutor to check that your conclusion ends with a clear, doable action.

activities.title: Refer to your sources as you present
activities.label: Activity 5: Refer to your sources as you present
activities.intro: A strong presenter always says where a fact came from. Practise turning your facts into sentences that refer to a real source.
steps: Write two facts that support your case, and beside each one, say where it came from.
Turn each one into a spoken sentence, starting with 'According to ...' or 'In my own survey of ...'.
Read both sentences aloud, and check they sound clear and natural.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two facts and their sources to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your structure was easy to follow, and where you referred to a source well.
Ask it to suggest one more way to refer to a source out loud.

activities.title: Think about your audience
activities.label: Activity 6: Think about your audience
activities.intro: The same case can be shared in different ways for different audiences, without changing the facts. Think about the different people you might present your issue to.
steps: Write which reason you would lead with for the school's leaders, and why.
Write which reason you would lead with for younger children, and why.
Write which reason you would lead with for your family, and why.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which reason you would lead with for each of your three audiences.
Ask it whether your choices make sense, and why.
Then ask the tutor to play one audience, so you can practise presenting to them.

activities.title: Use facts and opinions, and answer a concern fairly
activities.label: Activity 7: Use facts and opinions, and answer a concern fairly
activities.intro: A believable case mixes facts you can check with opinions you believe, and it is brave enough to answer a concern. Build this into the body of your presentation.
steps: Write two facts that support your case, and beside each one, say where it came from.
Write one opinion of your own, starting with 'I think ...' or 'I believe ...'.
Write the strongest concern someone might have about your idea, as fairly as you can.
Write your answer to it, starting with 'It is true that ...' and then 'However, ...'.

boxes.title: A model: answering a concern fairly
lines: The concern, stated fairly: it is true that the school only has a little money to spend, and lamps are not free.
The answer: however, five lamps would cost less than the school already spends on paper in a month, and every child would get a fair turn through a sign-out list.
Notice how answering the worry, instead of ignoring it, makes the case stronger and fairer.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your facts, your opinion, and your answer to the concern to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check that your facts really are facts and your opinion really is an opinion.
Ask the tutor to raise the concern back at you, so you can practise answering it out loud.

activities.title: Rehearse your presentation, then deliver it for real
activities.label: Activity 8: Rehearse your presentation, then deliver it for real
activities.intro:
This is the big one. Put your introduction, reasons and conclusion together into one short presentation, then rehearse it fully before you deliver it. Rehearsing with your AI tutor is exactly how nerves shrink and clarity grows.

As you rehearse, practise the way you deliver, not just the words. Speak a little more slowly than feels natural, so every word is clear. Pause after your key message, to let it land. Look up at your audience instead of only at your page.
steps: Put your whole case in order, following your skeleton plan.
Read it aloud once on your own, slowly and clearly.
Rehearse it with your AI tutor as your audience, at least twice, improving it each time.
Then deliver it for real in your teacher session, and if you can, to your family at home.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Present your whole case to your AI tutor from start to finish.
Ask it to be your audience and give you two stars and one wish: two things that worked and one thing to improve.
Then ask the tutor to tell your talk back to you, so you can check your key message came through clearly.

boxes.title: Deliver it for real
lines: Bring your presentation to your next teacher session and deliver it to a real audience.
Afterwards, present it to your family or a neighbour, and ask them what they understood and what they would ask.
Write down one thing that went well, and one thing you will do even better next time.

activities.title: Practise active listening and asking relevant questions
activities.label: Activity 9: Practise active listening and asking relevant questions
activities.intro:
Communication is two-way, so this last activity grows your listening. You will practise active listening and asking relevant questions, the kind that help you understand and gently test an idea.

Remember that a good question is a gift, not an attack. Asking 'How do you know that?' in a kind voice helps the speaker show their evidence, and helps everyone listening decide how much to trust the idea.
steps: Ask your AI tutor to present a short case for a solution to a local issue, playing a classmate.
As it speaks, annotate: jot quick notes and question marks next to anything you want to ask about.
Ask two relevant questions: one to understand (Could you explain ...?) and one to test the idea (How do you know that ...?).
Listen to the answers, then ask one follow-up question to clarify.

boxes.title: Good questions to ask a speaker
lines: Could you explain what you mean by ...?
What do you mean by ...?
How do you know that? Where did that come from?
Can you tell me a little more about that?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: After your listening practice, ask your AI tutor to rate your questions: were they relevant and clear?
Ask it to suggest one sharper question you could have asked.
Ask the tutor why asking 'How do you know that?' kindly can help a whole group, not just you.

boxes.title: Deliver it for real
lines: In your next teacher session, listen carefully to another learner's idea and ask them one relevant, kind question.
At home, ask a family member to tell you about an issue they care about, and practise asking two good questions.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 13 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'communication' mean?
practice.answer: Communication means presenting information so others understand it, by speaking or writing, and also listening to others and asking questions. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: Communication has two halves: presenting, and ______.
practice.answer: Listening.

practice.prompt: Name two ways you can present information to others.
practice.answer: Any two of: speaking, writing, showing a picture or a chart.

practice.prompt: What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?
practice.answer: A fact can be checked and shown to be true; an opinion is what someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a fact? (a) Solar lamps charge in sunlight (b) solar lamps are the best invention ever (c) our school should buy more lamps.
practice.answer: (a) Solar lamps charge in sunlight. It can be checked, so it is a fact.

practice.prompt: In a source, what is the difference between an argument and its supporting evidence?
practice.answer: An argument is the reason someone gives; the supporting evidence is the fact, detail or example that backs it up.

practice.prompt: A speaker who thinks about who they are talking to, and changes which reasons they lead with, is thinking about their ______.
practice.answer: Audience.

practice.prompt: Put the four parts of a skeleton plan in order: conclusion, a concern answered fairly, introduction, reasons.
practice.answer: Introduction, reasons, a concern answered fairly, conclusion.

practice.prompt: Why does a fair presentation include answering one concern people might have?
practice.answer: Because acknowledging a concern fairly, and then answering it, makes your case fairer and more convincing, and shows you have thought about more than your own side.

practice.prompt: Give one reason why a presenter should say where a fact came from.
practice.answer: Any one of: it shows you are not just making things up; it lets your audience trust and check your work; it makes your case more believable.

practice.prompt: Write one relevant question you could ask a speaker to understand their idea better.
practice.answer: Any relevant understanding question, such as: Could you explain what you mean by that? or Can you tell me a little more about that?

practice.prompt: What does active listening mean?
practice.answer: Listening with your full attention, on purpose, following the speaker's idea, and then asking a relevant question about what they said.

practice.prompt: Name two of the other five Global Perspectives skills that communication draws on.
practice.answer: Any two of: Research, Analysis, Evaluation, Reflection, Collaboration.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each communication word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Presenting
options: A. The people you are trying to reach when you present.
B. Sharing information so that others can understand it, by speaking or writing.
C. A reason someone gives to support their point of view.
D. The fact, detail or example that backs up an argument.
E. Paying full attention to what others say, so you understand them.
F. Truly about the matter in hand, and therefore useful.
practice.answer: B — Sharing information so that others can understand it, by speaking or writing.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Listening
practice.answer: E — Paying full attention to what others say, so you understand them.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Audience
practice.answer: A — The people you are trying to reach when you present.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Argument
practice.answer: C — A reason someone gives to support their point of view.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Evidence
practice.answer: D — The fact, detail or example that backs up an argument.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Relevant
practice.answer: F — Truly about the matter in hand, and therefore useful.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Samatar presents to the school leaders, and then to a Grade 1 class, about the same lamp scheme. Should he change his facts, or which reasons he leads with? Explain.
practice.answer: He should keep his facts the same, but change which reasons he leads with: cost and fairness for the leaders, and how the lamp works and the simple rules for the younger children.

practice.prompt: Amina says: 'Everyone knows solar lamps are the best thing ever.' Why is this weak, and how could she make it a strong, honest sentence?
practice.answer: It is an opinion dressed up as a fact, and 'the best thing ever' cannot be checked. A stronger version: solar lamps charge for free in sunlight, and my survey found that nine of fifteen classmates would use one.

practice.prompt: Hodan finishes her talk without saying what she wants to happen. Which part of her presentation is weak, and what should she add?
practice.answer: Her conclusion is weak, because she never says what she wants to happen. She should add a clear, doable action, such as: let us trial five lamps for one term.

practice.prompt: While Yusuf listens to a classmate's plan, he is not sure how it would work. What relevant question should he ask?
practice.answer: He should ask a relevant testing question, such as: How would your plan work, or where did that idea come from?

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own pace ...
Rehearsing with my AI tutor, my audience and practice partner ...
Delivering my work for real in my teacher session ...
Presenting to my family at home ...
Writing my plan down as I went ...
